title: BSOD triggered when AlwaysOnTop module is enabled, especially around display sleep/reconfiguration
summary: Always On Top has a credible BSOD report tied to display sleep/reconfiguration, and the public evidence is strong enough for a maintainer reproduction pass.
next_action: Run the maintainer-side reproduction plan on a multi-monitor DisplayPort setup before committing to a code-fix design.

confidence.rationale: The crash signature and repro narrative are detailed, but the PowerToys-side failing mechanism is still inferred rather than confirmed.

judgment.rationale: The issue already contains enough public detail to justify a focused reproduction attempt without asking the reporter for more generic logs.
evidence: The issue gives numbered reproduction steps around sleep, lock, and monitor power transitions.
The crash dumps reportedly share the same 0x7F double-fault signature in win32kbase!vUnreferencePdevWorker.
Disabling Always On Top stopped the crashes under the same display-cycling conditions.
A fresh PowerToys diagnostic ZIP was added after the first automated triage request.
judgment.recommended_action: Reproduce with Always On Top enabled on a multi-monitor system and inspect the module’s event/border handling around display teardown before drafting a repo-side fix.

fix_assessment.rationale: A repository change is plausible, but the current evidence is best used to reproduce and isolate the crash path first; the exact PowerToys-side fix is not yet scoped safely.

issue_context.summary: The reporter tied repeated BSODs during display sleep and monitor reconfiguration to Always On Top being enabled, with consistent crash signatures and a fresh follow-up bug report.
known_information: PowerToys 0.100.2 is installed from GitHub on Windows 11 build 26100.
The system uses a two-monitor DisplayPort setup and crashes during repeated display sleep/wake or monitor power-cycle transitions.
The crash analysis points to recursive win32k PDEV teardown exhausting the kernel stack.
Disabling Always On Top stopped the crashes while other modules remained enabled.
inferences: The failure is likely tied to how Always On Top reacts to window/display events during topology churn, but the exact callback or window-state operation is not proven from public evidence alone.
This looks reproducible enough for a maintainer to investigate locally without another reporter round-trip.
issue_context.analysis: The issue already clears the bar for a maintainer reproduction pass. The remaining uncertainty is technical and maintainer-side, not something the reporter can cheaply answer with another generic request.
initial_investigation: Always On Top subscribes to WinEvent callbacks for location, minimize, move/size, foreground, focus, and destroy events in src/modules/alwaysontop/AlwaysOnTop/AlwaysOnTop.cpp.
The module maintains topmost-window and border state but does not have an explicit display-topology transition handler in that code path.
No linked PR or existing ownership was found on the issue itself.

actions.label: Reproduce Always On Top display-sleep crash

reproduce.title: Exercise Always On Top during monitor topology changes
reproduce.version_requirement: PowerToys 0.100.2 or newer with Always On Top enabled
prerequisites: Windows desktop with at least two monitors, preferably DisplayPort-connected
Always On Top enabled; no specific pinned window required
setup: Use a profile where Always On Top is enabled and FancyZones is disabled, matching the reporter as closely as practical.
Keep crash dump capture enabled if available.
steps: Enable Always On Top and leave the module running in the background.
Repeatedly cycle through display sleep/wake, Win+L with display timeout, or power one monitor off while the other remains on.
Observe whether the machine bugchecks with the same 0x7F / win32kbase!vUnreferencePdevWorker signature.
reproduce.expected_result: Display topology changes should not crash the system; if a crash occurs, it should preserve the same kernel stack signature reported in the issue.
